analysis.one_liner: Bans insurance denials for preexisting conditions, creates a government-run health plan, and requires nearly everyone to carry coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared three House committees by votes of 26-22, 23-18, and 31-28 and was placed on the House calendar in October 2009, but the House never voted on it; its substance reached law five months later in the Affordable Care Act, minus the government-run plan.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the first full House version of the 2009 health reform law. It would have forbidden insurers from denying or dropping people for preexisting conditions, required every insurance plan to cover a standard set of benefits with yearly costs capped at $5,000 per person, created a marketplace where people could buy coverage with federal subsidies, and added a government-run insurance plan to compete with private ones. It paid for this with a tax on income above $350,000, requirements that employers contribute to coverage, and a tax penalty on people who stayed uninsured.
analysis.who_benefits: People without insurance or with preexisting health conditions, who could no longer be denied or dropped; low- and middle-income families, who would get sliding-scale subsidies to buy coverage; seniors, through smaller drug-coverage gaps and free preventive care; and small businesses with payrolls under $250,000, which are exempt from the employer requirement and get a coverage tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insurers from denying coverage or setting prices based on health status, and bans dropping policyholders except in cases of clear fraud.

Caps annual out-of-pocket costs at $5,000 per individual and $10,000 per family, bans annual and lifetime coverage limits, and requires plans to cover hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health, maternity care, and preventive services at no cost-sharing.

Creates a Health Insurance Exchange where individuals and employers can shop for plans, with an affordability premium credit and cost-sharing credit for low-income families, alongside a government-run public insurance option.
Expands Medicaid to more low-income individuals and families and reduces the Medicare Part D coverage gap.
Exempts businesses with payrolls below $250,000 from the employer requirement and gives small businesses a tax credit for employee coverage expenses.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals who remain uninsured pay a tax; employers that do not offer coverage make contributions toward employee coverage; taxpayers with income above $350,000 pay a surtax; accident and health insurance policies are taxed to finance research on which treatments work best; and hospitals and Medicare Advantage plans see Medicare payments reduced or restructured.
analysis.who_pays_short: The uninsured, large employers, and high earners

drawbacks.text: Everyone without coverage must buy a plan or pay a tax, a requirement that became the most contested part of the later law.
Employers face a coverage participation requirement with payroll-based contributions, which opponents argued would discourage hiring.
The financing rests partly on a surtax on individual income above $350,000, meaning the expansion depends on revenue from a narrow tax base that future Congresses could alter.

The bill is built around private insurance: subsidies flow through private plans in the Exchange, existing individual policies are grandfathered with strict limits on changes, and employer plans get a five-year grace period before they must meet the new benefit standards, so the industry that caused many of the problems remains the delivery channel.

The essential-benefits package is set by an advisory committee and the HHS Secretary through regulation, so actual covered benefits and costs would depend on later administrative decisions rather than the statute itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is sweeping: guaranteed access to coverage and real cost protections, financed by high earners, employers, and the uninsured who decline to buy in. The design weaknesses are real but secondary: the mandate pushes premiums toward insurers rather than a single public payer, the grandfathering rules mean many existing plans would change over time, and benefit details are left to regulators. On balance the bill would deliver much more in security to ordinary households than it costs them, which is why its main opponents were concentrated in the insurance industry and among high earners.

outcome.mechanism: Three House committees passed it and it was placed on the House calendar, but the House leadership never brought this bill to the floor and instead advanced a rewritten successor bill that became the vehicle for the eventual law.

narrative.text: Introduced on July 14, 2009 by Rep. John Dingell together with six other senior House Democrats, and referred to five committees the same day.

Three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — each reported the bill amended on October 14, 2009, after markups that produced narrow votes of 26-22, 23-18, and 31-28.
The Oversight and Government Reform and Budget committees were discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 168), the step that makes it available for floor debate.
The House never voted on H.R. 3200; no floor action or roll call appears anywhere in its action history after the October 14 placement on the calendar.

The House leadership instead brought up a rewritten successor bill (H.R. 3962), which the House passed in November 2009, and the final Affordable Care Act became law in March 2010 using a Senate bill as the vehicle.

The public health insurance option, the bill's most distinctive feature, did not survive into the final law; the enacted Affordable Care Act kept the preexisting-condition ban, the subsidies, and most other core provisions in a modified form.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers are better off than they would have been under this bill, because the government-run competitor it created was stripped out of the final law. High earners also paid a smaller tax than the bill's surtax. Tens of millions of uninsured people nonetheless gained coverage under the weaker law that eventually passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, spared the public option

for.name: Rep. John Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 14, 2009 with six other senior House Democrats and added three more sponsors when it was reported.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Held markups in July 2009 and reported the bill amended on October 14, 2009, after committee votes of 26-22 and 31-28.

for.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill amended on October 14, 2009, covering its tax and financing provisions.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Held markups and reported the bill amended on October 14, 2009.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Made health insurance reform his top legislative priority through 2009 and pressed Congress to pass a bill with a public option.

against.name: House Republican Conference
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill wholesale in committee and in the public debate over the summer of 2009; committee report votes were nearly unanimous against it.

against.name: Blue Dog Coalition
against.what_they_did: Extracted concessions and delayed the Energy and Commerce markup in late July 2009 over the bill's cost and structure, helping push final committee action to October.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 3200 to the House floor after it was placed on the calendar, choosing a rewritten successor bill instead.

against.name: America's Health Insurance Plans and allied insurers
against.what_they_did: Financed a sustained campaign against the public health insurance option through 2009, which contributed to its removal from the final law.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, but the committee votes that advanced the bill were razor-thin and nearly party-line — 26-22, 23-18, and 31-28 — with Republicans uniformly opposed and a bloc of conservative Democrats holding the margins slim.

industries.note: The bill subjects insurers to strict rules — no preexisting-condition denials, no rescissions except for fraud, required rebates if premiums are not spent on care — but also locks them in as the delivery channel by routing subsidies through their plans and requiring nearly everyone to buy their product. Its government-run public option is a direct competitive threat, which is why the industry fought the bill hardest on that provision.

Tens of millions of newly insured customers and a smaller Medicare Part D coverage gap increase drug demand, and the bill contains no Medicare price-negotiation mandate. New customers and better-covered patients rise together here.

The bill reduces Medicare Advantage payments and limits cost-sharing for beneficiaries, clawing back the above-cost subsidies these plans receive, with the savings folded into broader coverage expansion.

Expanded coverage sharply reduces uncompensated care, but hospitals also absorb Medicare payment reductions for excess readmissions. On net most hospital operators gained from reform, which is why large parts of the industry backed it.

industries.industry: Employers with payrolls above $250,000 that do not offer coverage
industries.note: These employers must either contribute toward employee coverage or pay into the Exchange for workers who use it; businesses below $250,000 are exempt.
The bill's main revenue source is a surtax on individual income above $350,000, placing the financing burden on the highest earners.
